name: Neri Oxman
bio: Neri Oxman (born 1976) is an architect, designer and researcher who coined the term 'Material Ecology' for design that is grown, computed and fabricated together with natural systems. She studied medicine and architecture in Israel and London before a PhD at MIT, where she founded the Mediated Matter group at the MIT Media Lab. Her work moves between the lab and the gallery: 3D-printed objects whose material properties vary across their surface (Raycounting, Monocoque, Beast), wearable pieces made with Iris van Herpen, printed glass, and structures made with living organisms, most famously the Silk Pavilion (2013), whose silk was spun by thousands of silkworms on a robotically woven frame. MoMA gave her a solo exhibition, 'Material Ecology', in 2020. That year she left MIT and founded the design company OXMAN in New York.
studyNotes: The organism is a collaborator. In the Silk Pavilion a robot lays down a scaffold and the silkworms finish it, so the final form is negotiated between a program and an animal's behaviour.

Variation across one material. Instead of assembling parts, she grades stiffness, colour or opacity continuously through a single printed object. Look at Monocoque and Beast and ask where the 'joints' have gone.
Computation as a way of reading nature. Many works start from a simulation of light, heat or force, then use that data to decide where material goes.
The lab and the museum are one practice. Prototypes, diagrams and research photos are shown alongside finished objects; the process is part of the work.

works.title: Silk Pavilion
works.medium: Silk spun by about 6,500 silkworms over a CNC-woven silk scaffold
works.note: A robot wove a base frame of silk threads, then the silkworms were released onto it and filled in the gaps, guided by light and heat.
